title: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
summary: How AlphaZero, STaR, ReST-EM, SPIN, Self-Rewarding LMs and Absolute Zero turn a model's own samples into better training data, and what each loop's filter or judge limits.
outcomes: Explain why self-generated data improves a model only when search, a verifier or a judge adds information
Trace an AlphaZero-style search and explain why training on visit counts sharpens the policy
Compute how samples per problem and success rate decide what a STaR or ReST-EM loop can learn
Estimate the share of lucky false-positive rationales a final-answer filter keeps
Compare SPIN, Self-Rewarding LMs and Absolute Zero by signal source and ceiling

lessons.title: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill

blocks.md: From the prerequisite courses you know two facts that seem to clash. RLVR with GRPO improves a model using rewards from an automatic checker. Model collapse shows that a model trained again and again on its own samples loses information, starting with rare cases. This course is about loops where a model does generate its own training data and still gets better. The central question for every method: **where does the new information come from?**

Every working loop has the same two steps. An **improvement operator** turns the current model into a stronger but slower or more expensive policy: a tree search, many samples filtered by a checker, or a judge that ranks answers. Then **distillation** trains the fast model to imitate that stronger policy. The improved model makes the operator stronger next round.

Anthony et al. (2017) named this **Expert Iteration** (ExIt): an *apprentice* (a neural network) imitates an *expert* (a tree search that uses the apprentice to guide it). AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero (Silver et al., 2017) run the same loop, starting from random weights and knowing only the game rules.

blocks.title: Expert iteration as AlphaZero runs it

nodes.label:
Network f(s)
outputs p and v

Targets per position:
search policy, outcome z

scenes.caption: The apprentice is one neural network. For a position s it outputs move probabilities p (an instant guess) and a value v (expected outcome). It starts from random weights.
The expert is a tree search that calls the network many times (800 simulations per move in AlphaZero). Looking ahead makes it stronger than the network alone, but far slower.
Both players pick moves with the search. At the end the game rules score the result: z is +1, 0 or -1. This outcome is the only ground truth in the loop.
Every position becomes a training example with two targets: the search's move distribution and the final outcome z.
Training pulls p toward the search policy and v toward z. The better network makes the next search stronger, which produces better targets: the loop closes.

blocks.caption: AlphaZero's loss for one position. (p, v) are the network's outputs, pi is the search's move distribution (visit counts), z the game outcome, c the weight-decay strength.

blocks.md: The cross-entropy term pulls the network's instant guess $\mathbf{p}$ toward $\pi$, the distribution of moves the search actually explored. The squared term pulls the value $v$ toward the real outcome $z$. Why is $\pi$ better than $\mathbf{p}$? Because the search combines the prior with look-ahead: it spends simulations on moves, measures how good they turn out, and shifts visits toward the ones that score well.

To see that shift with numbers, take one position with 4 legal moves. The network's prior is $P = (0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05)$ for moves a, b, c, d. In this simplified toy each move leads to a position whose value is fixed: 0.45, 0.70, 0.40, 0.30 (a real search expands a deep tree and gets values from the value head). Each simulation picks the move with the highest score under the pUCT rule used by the AlphaZero family, written here in MuZero's form:

blocks.tex: a^{*} = \arg\max_a \Big[ Q(a) + P(a)\,\frac{\sqrt{\sum_b N(b)}}{1 + N(a)} \Big( c_1 + \log \frac{\sum_b N(b) + c_2 + 1}{c_2} \Big) \Big]
blocks.caption: N(a) counts visits, Q(a) is the mean value seen (0 while unvisited). With c1 = 1.25 and c2 = 19652, the log term stays below 0.04 for 800 simulations, so the bonus is about 1.25 P(a) sqrt(total) / (1 + N(a)).

blocks.prompt: The prior favors move a (0.50) but move b is actually better (0.70 versus 0.45). After 800 simulations, roughly what share of the visits goes to b?
blocks.reveal: **711 of 800, or 0.889.** Move a gets only 68 (0.085). The prior decides where the first simulations go, but the bonus term decays like $1/(1+N)$ while $Q$ is a measured average, so after a few dozen visits the values dominate. The script that runs this rule exactly gives visits 68, 711, 17, 4.

blocks.title: Prior versus search visits at one position (toy)

scenes.caption: The network's prior p: it likes move a (0.50). Simplified toy: each move's result has a fixed value (a 0.45, b 0.70, c 0.40, d 0.30) instead of a deep search tree.
After 10 simulations: visits 4, 6, 0, 0. The prior sent the first simulation to a, but b's higher value already wins most visits.
After 50 simulations: 13, 34, 3, 0. The exploration bonus shrinks like 1/(1+N), so the measured value Q matters more with every visit.
After 200 simulations: 31, 160, 7, 2.
After 800 simulations: 68, 711, 17, 4. The visit distribution, 0.085 / 0.889 / 0.021 / 0.005, is the training target for p. It is a better policy than the prior.
Round 2, assuming training fits the target exactly: the new prior is the old visit share, and a fresh 800-simulation search gives 10, 788, 2, 0.
Round 3: 1, 799, 0, 0. The policy has sharpened onto b. Move d now has prior 0 and gets no visits at all, so if its value estimate were wrong the loop could never discover it.

blocks.md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

The last two scenes show the double edge. If the values are right, iterating sharpens the policy onto the best move. If an estimate is wrong, the loop can lock in the mistake, because a move with prior 0 gets no exploration bonus. AlphaZero counters this by adding Dirichlet noise to the root prior (with $\alpha$ = 0.3, 0.15 and 0.03 for chess, shogi and Go) and by sampling training moves in proportion to visit counts.

AlphaGo Zero also *gated* each new network: it replaced the best player only if it won by a 55% margin. AlphaZero dropped the gate and keeps updating one network. Trained for 700,000 steps of 4,096 positions, it passed Stockfish in chess after about 4 hours (300,000 steps).

A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

blocks.question: Why does training the policy head on MCTS visit counts improve the network instead of just copying it?
options: Visit counts are smoother than the prior, so the cross-entropy loss is lower
The search samples at a higher temperature, so the targets are more diverse
The search mixes the prior with measured look-ahead values, so the visit counts differ from the prior where look-ahead finds better moves
The visit counts include moves from human expert games
blocks.explain: The search is an improvement operator: it starts from the prior and moves visits toward moves whose measured values are higher. In the toy, the prior said 0.30 for b and the search said 0.889. Imitating that difference is the improvement. AlphaZero uses no human games.

blocks.question: After three rounds in the toy, move d has prior 0. Suppose d was actually the best move and its value estimate was wrong. What happens in later rounds without exploration noise?
options: d is never visited, because its exploration bonus is P(d) times something, which is 0, and its Q stays 0
800 simulations are enough that the search reaches d eventually
The value loss on z will raise P(d) automatically
The gate at 55% will reject the network and restore d
blocks.explain: The pUCT bonus is proportional to the prior. With P(d) = 0 and an unvisited Q of 0, d never has the highest score, so the search never looks at it and the outcome z never reflects it. This is exactly why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior during self-play.

lessons.title: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune

blocks.md: Language reasoning has no game tree, but it has a cheap improvement operator when answers can be checked: **sample several solutions, keep only those whose final answer is correct, and fine-tune on them**. The filtered set is better than what the model produces on average, so imitating it is an improvement, exactly like imitating the search in lesson 1.

**STaR**, the Self-Taught Reasoner (Zelikman et al., 2022), was the first version for chain-of-thought. It used GPT-J (6B parameters), a few-shot prompt of about 10 hand-written rationales, and datasets with answers but no rationales. It adds **rationalization**: for a question the model gets wrong, give it the correct answer as a hint, ask for a rationale, and keep it if it reaches that answer, as if no hint had been given.

blocks.title: One STaR iteration on three questions (simplified)

scenes.caption: STaR starts from a pretrained model M and a dataset of questions with known answers but no rationales. A few-shot prompt with about 10 worked rationales makes M write a rationale before answering.
Question 1: the model's rationale ends in answer b, which matches the key. The rationale is kept.
Question 2: the model answers d, the key says a. Rationalization: show the correct answer as a hint and ask for a rationale. It reaches a, so it is kept, stored without the hint.
Question 3: wrong without the hint and still wrong with it. Nothing is kept, so this question gives no training signal this round.
Fine-tune on the kept rationales, starting again from the original M rather than from the last checkpoint, then repeat with the new model generating the data.

blocks.tex: \nabla J = \sum_i \mathbb{E}_{\hat r_i, \hat y_i \sim p_M(\cdot \mid x_i)} \big[ \mathbb{1}(\hat y_i = y_i)\, \nabla \log p_M(\hat y_i, \hat r_i \mid x_i) \big]
blocks.caption: The STaR paper's view: this is the policy gradient for a 0/1 correctness reward. The indicator throws away the gradient of every wrong sample, which is exactly the filtering step.

blocks.md: So STaR is a crude form of the RL you know from GRPO: reward 1 for correct, 0 otherwise, but with no baseline, no negative signal from wrong answers, and many gradient steps on one batch of samples. Rationalization exists because without it the loop stalls: a question the model never solves never enters the training set. On CommonsenseQA (5-way multiple choice) the results were: few-shot chain-of-thought GPT-J 36.6%, GPT-J fine-tuned to answer directly 60.0%, STaR without rationalization 68.8%, STaR with it 72.5%, close to 73.0% for a fine-tuned GPT-3 that is 30x larger.

Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

**ReST-EM** (Singh et al., 2023) scales the idea up. Instead of one greedy sample, draw many temperature samples per problem: 32 for MATH and 64 for APPS, with top-K 40 and temperature 0.7. A binary reward checks the final answer (MATH) or runs test cases (APPS). Keep at most 10 correct solutions per problem, fine-tune the base model on them, and repeat. ReST-EM drops rationalization.

blocks.tex: q_{t+1}(y \mid x) \propto r(x,y)\, p_{\theta_t}(y \mid x), \qquad \theta_{t+1} = \arg\max_\theta \ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\theta_t}} \big[ r(x,y) \log p_\theta(y \mid x) \big]
blocks.caption: ReST-EM as expectation-maximization. E-step: reweight the current model's samples by reward (with 0/1 rewards: keep the correct ones). M-step: maximize reward-weighted log-likelihood (fine-tune on them).

blocks.md: Unlike online RL, sampling uses a model that stays fixed for the whole iteration, so data collection and training are decoupled: generate one big dataset, then train on it. The ReST-EM paper notes this makes the method easier to scale to very large models.

blocks.prompt: Five problems have per-sample success rates 0.9, 0.5, 0.1, 0.02 and 0. With one sample each, the expected number of problems that contribute a correct solution is 0.9 + 0.5 + 0.1 + 0.02 + 0 = 1.52. What is it with 32 samples each?
blocks.reveal: **3.44.** Each problem contributes with probability $1-(1-p)^{32}$: 1.000, 1.000, 0.966, 0.476 and 0. More samples mostly help the hard problems, which is where new skill comes from. The problem with $p = 0$ stays at 0: no amount of sampling helps, which is why STaR added rationalization.

blocks.title: Chance that a problem yields at least one correct sample

scenes.caption: With one sample per problem, a problem the model solves 10% of the time contributes a training example only 10% of the time.
With N = 8 the same problem yields a correct solution with probability 0.570.
N = 32, as ReST-EM uses on MATH: 0.966 for p = 0.1 and 0.476 for p = 0.02. More samples reach further into the hard tail.
N = 64, as ReST-EM uses on APPS: 0.726 for p = 0.02. But at p = 0 the curve is 0 for every N: sampling cannot find what the model never produces.

blocks.title: Sample, check, cap: one seeded draw of 8 samples

scenes.caption: Five training problems, 8 samples each (shown small; ReST-EM draws 32 or 64). Each sample is a full solution whose final answer will be checked.
The checker marks each sample. This seeded draw got 7, 4, 1, 0 and 0 correct. P4 is solvable in principle (p = 0.02) but was unlucky; P5 never will be.
Cap at 3 correct per problem (ReST-EM caps at 10). P1's extra 4 correct samples are dropped, so the easy problem no longer dominates the fine-tuning set.

blocks.md: Why cap at 10? With 32 samples the expected number of correct solutions is 28.8, 16, 3.2, 0.64 and 0 for our five problems, so the easiest problem would be 59% of the fine-tuning data. With the cap, the expected kept counts are 10, 9.99, 3.2, 0.64 and 0, and the shares become 42%, 42%, 13% and 3%. The two hard problems double their weight.

Results: on PaLM 2 models, fine-tuning on ReST-EM's self-generated solutions beat fine-tuning on human-written solutions for MATH and APPS, and the gain was larger for the bigger model. But most of the improvement came in the first iteration. Training accuracy kept rising with more iterations while test accuracy flattened on MATH and dropped on APPS in iteration 2, which the authors attribute to overfitting a small set of training problems (7,500 for MATH, 2,342 for APPS).

blocks.question: Your ReST-EM run uses 64 samples per problem, yet 20% of training problems never get a correct sample. Which change gives the model a training signal on exactly those problems?
options: Train for more epochs on the solutions you already kept
Lower the sampling temperature so solutions are more careful
Continue fine-tuning from the last checkpoint instead of the base model
STaR's rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and keep rationales that reach it
blocks.explain: Problems with no correct sample are invisible to the filter; more training on kept data or lower temperature cannot add them. Rationalization samples from a different distribution, p(r | x, y), which can reach the answer. The cost, covered in lesson 3, is more rationales that reach the right answer for the wrong reasons.

blocks.question: Why does ReST-EM cap the number of correct solutions kept per problem?
options: Easy problems produce many more correct samples, so without a cap they would dominate the fine-tuning set
Storage: 64 solutions per problem would not fit in memory
The verifier becomes unreliable after 10 solutions
To keep the dataset exactly the same size every iteration
blocks.explain: With 32 samples, a problem solved 90% of the time contributes about 28.8 solutions and one solved 10% of the time about 3.2. The cap of 10 rebalances the data toward harder problems; the paper says it keeps diversity and prevents overfitting to easy problems.

lessons.title: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting

blocks.md: In lessons 1 and 2 the filter is the only thing that adds information. So its errors go straight into the training set. A final-answer check accepts a solution whose reasoning is wrong but whose answer happens to match: a **false positive**. Cobbe et al., who built GSM8K and trained verifiers on it, point out exactly this: labeling solutions only by the final answer means some flawed solutions are labeled correct.

blocks.prompt: A model answers 5-way multiple-choice questions. On 30% of questions it reasons soundly and gets them right. On the rest its reasoning is flawed and its answer is effectively a random pick among the 5 options. What fraction of the rationales a STaR filter keeps are flawed?
blocks.reveal: **About 32%.** Out of 50 questions: 15 sound and correct, and 35 flawed of which $35 \times 0.2 = 7$ match the key by luck. The filter keeps $15 + 7 = 22$, and $7/22 = 0.318$. The STaR paper notes this risk directly: on CommonsenseQA a random pick is right about 20% of the time regardless of the reasoning.

scenes.caption: 50 five-way questions, one sample each. The filter keeps every rationale whose final answer matches the key: 22 of them. The filter cannot tell them apart.
Inside: 15 come from sound reasoning (30% of 50). The other 35 had flawed reasoning and guessed among 5 options, so about 7 landed on the key by luck. 7 of 22 is 31.8% of the training data.
Fine-tuning treats all 22 alike. The 7 lucky ones teach the model that plausible but wrong reasoning ending in the right letter is good reasoning.

blocks.caption: q is the rate of sound reasoning, c the chance a flawed attempt still lands on the right answer. Simplified: it assumes flawed attempts guess uniformly.

blocks.title: Share of kept rationales that are lucky guesses

params.name: c
params.label: chance a guess is right, c

scenes.caption: Five-way multiple choice (c = 0.2). Early in training, when q is small, lucky guesses are a large part of the kept data: 64% at q = 0.1 and 31.8% at q = 0.3.
Four options (c = 0.25): worse at every q, for example 36.8% at q = 0.3.
A numeric answer that is hard to guess (c = 0.01): 2.3% at q = 0.3. A large answer space makes the same filter far more precise. Simplified: real flawed reasoning is not a uniform guess.

blocks.md: Two experimental findings fit this picture. STaR tried a natural alternative to rationalization, sampling more at higher temperature, and found it counterproductive: it raised the chance of a correct answer from wrong reasoning, and training on that reasoning hurt generalization. ReST-EM reports that in preliminary experiments rationalization substantially increased false positives, correct answers with incorrect reasoning, which is one reason it uses plain sampling instead. Giving the model the answer makes it easier to write any story that ends there.

Prefer checks with a large answer space and several independent conditions. A numeric answer or a program that must pass a set of unit tests is rarely right by luck; a single multiple-choice letter often is. When a checker is weak, also inspect samples of the kept data by hand.

The second failure mode appears when the filter is a learned **reward model** instead of an exact check. ReST (Gulcehre et al., 2023), the predecessor of ReST-EM, trained machine translation with a learned quality metric as reward. It alternates a *Grow* step (sample a dataset from the policy) with several *Improve* steps that fine-tune on samples above a threshold $\tau$, raising $\tau$ each time. Reward model scores kept rising with more Grow steps, but human raters preferred the model after **one** Grow step. The authors warn that the risk of overfitting to the reward model grows with repeated Grow steps.

The third failure mode is plain overfitting. A verifier only adds information about the problems you have. In ReST-EM, training accuracy rose steadily across iterations while test accuracy stalled on MATH and fell on APPS in iteration 2. Compare model collapse from the prerequisite course: there the loop added no information at all. Here it adds some each round, but always about the same finite set of problems.

A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

blocks.question: For which task would a STaR-style final-answer filter keep the fewest flawed rationales, for the same model accuracy?
options: True or false questions
5-way multiple choice questions
Competition math problems with an integer answer
Open-ended summaries scored by a learned reward model
blocks.explain: The flawed share depends on c, the chance a flawed attempt matches anyway. It is 0.5 for true or false, 0.2 for 5 options, and tiny for an integer answer. A learned reward model adds its own errors on top, as ReST's human evaluation showed.

blocks.question: In ReST, reward model scores keep rising with every Grow step, but human raters prefer the model after one Grow step. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy is increasingly exploiting errors in the learned reward model, a proxy for human judgment
Human raters are noisier than the reward model, so their results should be ignored
The Improve thresholds were set too low
Translation quality cannot improve after one Grow step for any method
blocks.explain: The reward model is only a proxy. Optimizing a proxy harder eventually finds outputs it overrates. The ReST authors say exactly this and suggest periodically refreshing the reward model with human labels on the newest policy's outputs.

lessons.title: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs

blocks.md: Lessons 2 and 3 needed answers you can check. For open-ended chat there is no answer key. Two methods replace it with something already at hand. **SPIN** uses the existing human SFT data as the target. **Self-Rewarding LMs** use the model itself as the judge.

**SPIN**, Self-Play fIne-tuNing (Chen et al., 2024), starts from a supervised fine-tuned model. For each prompt $x$ in the SFT data, the previous iteration's model generates a response $y'$. The new model is trained to tell the human response $y$ apart from $y'$. The paper frames this as a game between two copies of one LLM: the *main player* (new model) learns to distinguish, the *opponent* (old model) tries to produce responses that cannot be distinguished. Next iteration, the new model becomes the opponent.

blocks.caption: y is the human response, y' is a sample from the previous model p_theta_t, lambda > 0 controls how far one iteration moves.

blocks.md: This is the DPO loss with three substitutions: the reference model is the previous iteration, the *chosen* response is always the human one, and the *rejected* response is always the model's own sample. No preference labels or reward model are needed. In an idealized setting where the model can be any distribution, the paper proves the loss is minimized only when $p_{\theta_t} = p_{\text{data}}$, and derives how one iteration moves the opponent:

blocks.tex: p_{t+1}(y \mid x) \ \propto\ p_t(y \mid x) \left( \frac{p_{\text{data}}(y \mid x)}{p_t(y \mid x)} \right)^{1/\lambda}
blocks.caption: Responses the model under-produces relative to the data gain probability; over-produced ones lose it. Smaller lambda moves faster; lambda = 1 jumps straight to p_data in this idealized form.

blocks.title: SPIN's ideal update pulls the model toward the data (lambda = 2)

scenes.caption: Simplified: a prompt with only 4 possible responses. The human SFT data has p_data = 0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05.
The SFT model p_0 is off: 0.20, 0.20, 0.30, 0.30. Total variation distance from the data (half the sum of absolute differences): 0.40.
Iteration 1 multiplies each probability by (p_data / p_0)^(1/2) and renormalizes: 0.353, 0.273, 0.237, 0.137. Distance 0.174.
Iteration 3: 0.466, 0.298, 0.171, 0.065. Distance 0.036, roughly halving each time.
Iteration 4: 0.483, 0.299, 0.160, 0.057. Distance 0.018. Each step changes less, because the ratio p_data / p_t approaches 1, the same shrinking gains the SPIN paper observed.

blocks.md: SPIN's fixed point is the human data distribution. It can extract more from an SFT dataset than plain SFT does, but it cannot surpass that data: once the model's responses are indistinguishable from the human ones, the loss gives no signal.

Experiments: SPIN fine-tuned zephyr-7b-sft-full (a Mistral-7B SFT model) using 50k prompts sampled from UltraChat200k, training 2 epochs per iteration. The average score on the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard tasks rose from 58.14 to 63.16 and MT-Bench from 5.94 to 6.78, with each iteration adding less than the one before. Continued plain SFT on the same data had plateaued or got worse.

**Self-Rewarding Language Models** (Yuan et al., 2024) go further: the model writes the preferences too. Starting from Llama 2 70B fine-tuned on 3,200 human instruction examples plus 1,630 examples of judging responses (both from Open Assistant), each iteration runs the loop below. The judge prompt adds one point per criterion met: relevance, partial coverage, a useful answer, a clear and well-organized assistant response, and expert, tailored quality.

scenes.caption: New prompts come from few-shot prompting in the Self-Instruct style. In the main experiments a fixed model (Llama 2-Chat 70B) writes them; an appendix shows the trained model can do it too.
The current model samples N = 4 candidate responses at temperature 0.7.
The same weights, prompted as a judge, score each response out of 5 with an additive rubric, 3 times with sampling, and average the scores.
Highest and lowest scored responses form a preference pair. If they tie, the prompt is discarded.
DPO on these pairs (beta 0.1) produces M(t+1), which is a better responder and a better judge for the next round.

blocks.md: A worked pair: four responses to one prompt receive judge samples (4, 3, 4), (5, 4, 5), (2, 3, 3) and (4, 5, 4). The averages are 3.67, 4.67, 2.67 and 4.33. The pair is response 2 (chosen) versus response 3 (rejected). If all four had averaged the same, the prompt would yield no pair. Iteration 1 produced 3,964 pairs to train M2, iteration 2 produced 6,942 pairs to train M3.

scenes.caption: AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4 Turbo, judged by GPT-4 Turbo: 9.94%, 15.38%, 20.44%.
As a judge, agreement with human rankings on held-out pairs: 78.7%, 80.4%, 81.7% (an SFT model trained without judge data scored 65.1%). Policy and judge improve together.

blocks.md: Rising numbers are not proof that quality rose. Average response length on AlpacaEval grew from 1092 (M1) to 1552 (M2) to 2552 (M3), and length is known to correlate with judged quality. The authors list reward hacking within the framework as an open question, and note that LLMs supply both the training reward and (through GPT-4) the evaluation, which needs deeper analysis.

blocks.question: In SPIN's idealized update, set lambda = 1. What happens after one iteration?
options: The model moves halfway toward the data distribution
The model becomes exactly p_data, and further iterations change nothing
The model overshoots p_data and oscillates
Nothing, because lambda = 1 cancels the loss
blocks.explain: With 1/lambda = 1 the update is p_t times p_data / p_t, which is p_data after renormalizing. Then the ratio is 1 everywhere and the update is the identity. Real training cannot represent the ideal update exactly, which is one reason SPIN needs several iterations.

blocks.question: Why can Self-Rewarding training, at least in principle, raise its own ceiling, while SPIN cannot exceed its SFT data?
options: Self-Rewarding uses DPO and SPIN does not
Self-Rewarding trains on more prompts
In Self-Rewarding the judge is the model being trained, so its preferences can improve each iteration; SPIN always treats the fixed human response as the winner
SPIN uses a smaller base model
blocks.explain: Both losses are DPO-like. The difference is the target: SPIN's chosen response is always from the fixed human data, so p_data is the fixed point. Self-Rewarding's preferences come from a judge that is retrained every iteration, which is also why it carries a risk of reward hacking that SPIN does not.

lessons.title: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop

blocks.md: Every loop so far needs a fixed set of prompts or problems. **Absolute Zero** (Zhao et al., 2025) removes that too: one model *proposes* tasks and *solves* them, and a Python executor both validates the tasks and checks the answers. It uses RLVR, as in your GRPO course, but on a curriculum the model writes for itself. A task is a triplet of program $p$, input $i$ and output $o = p(i)$.

scenes.caption: Proposer role: conditioned on a task type and K = 6 past examples from the buffer, the model writes a new program and input, asked to differ from the examples.
The executor runs it. The task is valid only if it runs and returns a value, avoids banned modules such as os.sys, sys and shutil, and returns the same output on 2 runs (a cheap determinism check).
The executor's output o completes the triplet (p, i, o). Hiding one part makes a task: predict o (deduction), find an input giving o (abduction), or write p from example pairs (induction).
Solver role: the same model answers. Python checks it by value equality; for abduction it checks p(guess) = p(true input), since many inputs can give the same output.
Both roles are rewarded and updated together. The only external signal is the Python executor; there is no human data beyond a trivial seed triplet (the identity function).

blocks.md: The proposer needs a reward that says which tasks are worth practicing. Absolute Zero estimates **learnability** with the solver itself: run $G$ solver rollouts on the new task (8 in their settings) and measure the average success $\bar r_{\text{solve}}$.

blocks.caption: A task nobody solves teaches nothing; a task everyone solves teaches nothing. Between those, harder is better.

blocks.prompt: Four proposed tasks are solved 0, 1, 4 and 8 times out of 8 rollouts. Which earns the proposer the highest reward?
blocks.reveal: **The task solved 1 time out of 8**, with reward $1 - 1/8 = 0.875$. The 4/8 task earns 0.5, and both 0/8 and 8/8 earn 0. The reward is not centered on 50%: it favors the hardest tasks that are still within reach, the frontier where the solver has something to learn.

blocks.title: Proposer reward versus solver success over 8 rollouts

scenes.caption: The learnability reward for each possible outcome of 8 solver rollouts. Unsolvable (0/8) and trivial (8/8) tasks both earn 0.
The best task is the hardest one the solver still sometimes solves: 1/8 earns 0.875, 4/8 earns 0.5. These are also exactly the groups where GRPO-style advantages are nonzero.

blocks.md: This mirrors what you know from GRPO: in a group of rollouts that all get the same reward, every advantage is zero and the group produces no gradient. Absolute Zero normalizes rewards with **Task-Relative REINFORCE++** (TRR++): a separate mean and standard deviation for each of the six combinations of task type and role, which the paper describes as a middle ground between GRPO's per-question baseline and one global baseline. A well-formatted wrong answer gets -0.5, and a formatting error gets -1; for the proposer, an invalid task counts as a formatting error.

Results: trained from Qwen2.5 base models with no human-curated tasks, the paper reports math gains of 10.9 points (base 7B) and 15.2 points (coder 7B) on their benchmark average, compared with 0.65 for code models trained with RLVR on expert-curated code data. Gains grew with model size: +5.7, +10.2 and +13.2 overall for 3B, 7B and 14B coder models. They also report an "uh-oh moment": with Llama 3.1 8B, the model occasionally wrote concerning chains of thought, which they flag for safety work.

"Zero data" does not mean zero prior knowledge. The model is a pretrained LLM, and the coder base model, which started 3.6 points lower in math, ended 0.7 points above the general base. The executor is the external signal; it can only certify what running deterministic Python can check.

Now compare the whole family by asking where the signal comes from and what caps it:

- **AlphaZero**: search plus exact game outcomes. Capped by search and network capacity, not by data.
- **STaR, ReST-EM**: an answer key or unit tests. Capped by the problem set and by lucky false positives.
- **ReST**: a learned reward model. Capped by how faithful that proxy is.
- **SPIN**: the human SFT responses. Capped by the data distribution itself.
- **Self-Rewarding**: the model's own judgment. Capped by the judge, with risk of reward hacking.
- **Absolute Zero**: a code executor. Capped by what execution can verify.

For any self-improvement claim, ask two questions: what outside the current model decides that a sample is good, and how often is it wrong? The loop can only improve as far as that signal is informative.

blocks.question: An Absolute Zero proposer writes a program that calls random.random() and returns the result. What happens to this proposal?
options: It becomes a hard abduction task, so the proposer gets a high learnability reward
It fails validation (random is a forbidden module, and two runs would give different outputs anyway), so it counts as a formatting error with reward -1
The solver gets credit for any numeric answer between 0 and 1
It is accepted, but only as an induction task
blocks.explain: Absolute Zero only accepts deterministic programs: it bans modules such as random and datetime outright, and it also runs each program twice (j = 2) and compares outputs. Only proposals that produce valid triplets count as correctly formatted, so this one gets the -1 penalty, which teaches the proposer to avoid unverifiable tasks.

blocks.question: A team wants a model to improve its customer-support replies, has thousands of real customer questions, and has no answer key or human preference labels. Which loop fits, and what is the main risk to monitor?
options: ReST-EM with a binary correctness reward; the risk is overfitting a small problem set
AlphaZero-style tree search; the risk is lack of exploration noise
Absolute Zero; the risk is nondeterministic programs
Self-Rewarding with the model as judge; the risk is the policy exploiting the judge, for example by growing longer replies
blocks.explain: Without checkable answers, the options are a judge or a human target. Self-Rewarding needs only prompts and a seed of judging examples. Its documented risk is that the judge's biases get amplified: the paper itself saw average response length grow about 2.3x over two iterations and flagged reward hacking.
